item.title: Two drown in search for water in Hela
item.description: Two primary school students have tragically drowned in the Koroba-Lake Kopiago district of Hela after a search for drinking water ended in disaster due to the ongoing El Niño drought. The victims, aged seven and 14, were both students at Guala Primary School in the South Koroba local level government [LLG].
item.content:encoded:
Two primary school students have tragically drowned in the Koroba-Lake Kopiago district of Hela after a search for drinking water ended in disaster due to the ongoing El Niño drought.

The victims, aged seven and 14, were both students at Guala Primary School in the South Koroba local level government [LLG].

Family spokesman Niki Adali said the school was forced to send students home early at lunchtime due to a severe water shortage affecting the institution.

Following their dismissal, a group of students [all relatives] walked to a nearby swampy area known as Kunu Tuku, where a small body of water had formed.

Adali explained that while swimming, the seven-year-old boy began struggling and started to sink. His 14-year-old relative immediately swam out to rescue him.

“He managed to pull him out and was carrying him back toward the shore, but just before reaching safety, both of them went under,” Adali said.

It is believed the older student succumbed to severe muscle cramps while attempting the rescue.

Police officers from Mobile Squad 22 [MS 22], led by Commander Jonathan Lakaio, visited the scene to assess the situation. Community members confirmed to police that the drownings were accidental and ruled out any foul play.

Stressing the severe impact of the drought on the community, Adali appealed to the Hela provincial government and the Koroba-Lake Kopiago District Development Authority [KLK DDA] for urgent assistance.

He urged authorities to supply water tanks to the Guala community, which hosts the primary school, a Catholic Biblical Centre [CBC] mission station, and the proposed Guala Nursing College.

He also appealed to the National Government for emergency relief, stating that most local creeks and small water sources in the swamp-surrounded area have completely dried up.

KLK DDA chief executive officer Stanley Kotange expressed sorrow over the tragedy, confirming he would present the community's plea to relevant authorities.

“On behalf of the district administration, Hela Governor Philip Undialu, and local MP William Bando, we extend our deepest condolences to the grieving families,” Kotange said.

“The DDA, under the leadership of MP Bando, will assist in ensuring the two children are given a proper burial.”

item.title: Buimo CS clinic gets medical supplies
item.description: The Buimo Correctional Services clinic in Lae received a fresh supply of essential medicines and medical consumables yesterday, fulfilling a pledge made by the Nawaeb District Development Authority [DDA] during Easter this year. Officer-in-charge Health Extension Officer [HEO] Derrick Wai collected the supplies on behalf of the facility, which will allow health workers to continue providing medica
item.content:encoded:
The Buimo Correctional Services clinic in Lae received a fresh supply of essential medicines and medical consumables yesterday, fulfilling a pledge made by the Nawaeb District Development Authority [DDA] during Easter this year.

Officer-in-charge Health Extension Officer [HEO] Derrick Wai collected the supplies on behalf of the facility, which will allow health workers to continue providing medical care to the surrounding community and correctional institution.

Wai expressed his gratitude to the DDA and urged other district authorities across the province to step up and support health facilities facing similar logistical constraints.

“The clinic is limited in its supplies due to the large population that relies on this facility,” Wai said.

“This small clinic caters for inmates from all 10 districts in Morobe, as well as neighbouring provinces.”

Nawaeb MP and DDA chairman Theo Pelgen said the intervention was part of a district-wide effort to ensure no community is left behind in basic service delivery.

“Inmates deserve equal treatment like everyone else, and they are included in the projects we are rolling out in the district,” Pelgen said.

“Access to essential medicines is a basic service that every family deserves. The district will continue investing in healthcare while working closely with the Morobe Provincial Health Authority and the National Department of Health to strengthen medicine supply chains.”

The distribution was carried out under the district-funded District Medicine Support Program, an initiative spearheaded by the DDA to cushion the impact of stockouts and delivery delays from the national level.

Under the initiative, the Nawaeb DDA directly procures and distributes emergency medical supplies to health centres and aid posts across the district to prevent life-saving drugs from running out.

item.title: 30 children undergo heart screening in Bougainville
item.description: 30 children in the Autonomous Region of Bougainville [AROB] have undergone specialized cardiac checks as part of the 2026 National Paediatric Cardiac Screening Program. The two-day screening clinic was conducted from July 27–28 at Buka General Hospital.
item.content:encoded:
30 children in the Autonomous Region of Bougainville [AROB] have undergone specialized cardiac checks as part of the 2026 National Paediatric Cardiac Screening Program.

The two-day screening clinic was conducted from July 27–28 at Buka General Hospital.

Specialist paediatrician Dr Kunera Kiromat led the program alongside prominent local paediatrician Dr Mathias Tovilu and health extension officer Delourdes Patuai.

The visit was important step for Dr Kiromat, being her first independent screening visit where she managed all 30 paediatric cases.

Out of the 30 children evaluated; 10 were given a clean bill of health with normal heart function, two were diagnosed with complex cardiac conditions requiring ongoing medical monitoring, one child was identified for review by the OpenHeart Surgical Mission for potential surgery, and, a post-operative patient was reviewed following a patent ductus arteriosus [PDA] post-ligation procedure.

Dr Tovilu said the annual outreach provided a vital opportunity to identify children who needed specialized care and potential referral to Port Moresby for surgery.

“It also ensures that children with more complex heart conditions, including rheumatic heart disease, are reviewed by specialists and connected to the most suitable care pathway,” Dr Tovilu said.

“While not every child with a congenital heart condition will require surgery, the program helps prioritize those who are most likely to benefit from timely intervention, supporting better outcomes and ongoing care for children and their families.”

Bougainville is the seventh province visited under the national program this year, following earlier visits to Hela, Northern, Milne Bay, Jiwaka, Western Highlands, and Madang.

The screening in Buka was made possible through support from Buka General Hospital, Air Niugini, BSP Financial Group Limited, and the Sir Brian Bell Foundation.

The national screening team will head to East Sepik and Southern Highlands provinces next month, before traveling to East New Britain in September.

item.title: Superannuation body demands urgent action on long-awaited sector reforms
item.description: The Association of Superannuation Funds of Papua New Guinea [ASFPNG] has called on the Government to urgently act on long-standing superannuation reforms to protect workers' savings and safeguard the financial system. ASFPNG in a media statement, said despite extensive consultations and reviews over the years, key policy, legislative, and taxation issues affecting superannuation members remain unr
item.content:encoded:
The Association of Superannuation Funds of Papua New Guinea [ASFPNG] has called on the Government to urgently act on long-standing superannuation reforms to protect workers' savings and safeguard the financial system.

ASFPNG in a media statement, said despite extensive consultations and reviews over the years, key policy, legislative, and taxation issues affecting superannuation members remain unresolved.

The association raised concerns over the delay of the Superannuation and Life Insurance Review Report, which was commissioned to address key issues such as compulsory super coverage, contribution adequacy, preservation ages, and taxation.

The report is currently before Treasurer Ian Ling-Stuckey.

ASFPNG president and Nasfund chief executive officer Rajeev Sharma said the focus must shift to immediate implementation.

“The priority now must be implementation,” Sharma said. “Further delay will continue to reduce the retirement outcomes of members and weaken confidence in the reform process.”

ASFPNG outlined several priority areas needing government action, including:

Super for all: Extending compulsory superannuation coverage to all eligible workers, including those in businesses with fewer than 15 employees, and removing waiting periods.

Contribution rates: Reviewing and gradually increasing the statutory employer contribution rate, which has remained fixed at 8.4 per cent for years.

Preserving savings: Restricting early unemployment withdrawals to employee contributions while preserving employer funds to maintain long-term compound growth.

Tax reduction: Lowering the 25 per cent tax on superannuation investment income to regional standards to improve real growth for members.

Unpaid entitlements: Giving unpaid employer superannuation contributions higher priority status under law during business insolvencies and enforcement proceedings.

ASFPNG also expressed serious concern regarding proposed tax amendments that would grant the Internal Revenue Commission [IRC] expanded powers to garnish money directly from customer bank accounts.

The association says allowing state garnishee powers to override existing bank mortgages or secured creditor rights could destabilise the banking sector.

“Where statutory garnishee rights take priority over a bank’s mortgage or security interests, the potential consequences include increased loan-loss provisioning, stricter lending, higher interest rates, and reduced access to credit,” ASFPNG stated.

Because superannuation funds hold major investments in PNG’s commercial banks, any negative impact on bank profitability directly harms investment returns meant for members.

ASFPNG urged structured engagement between the Department of Treasury, Bank of Papua New Guinea, the IRC, commercial banks, and super funds to ensure a fair and safe outcome for all stakeholders.

item.title: Veteran mariner calls for safer sea travel as rough weather peaks
item.description: Papua New Guinea is now in the most dangerous period of the year for sea travel, and veteran Chief Marine Pilot Captain Max Stossel is urging people to avoid unnecessary journeys as rough weather continues across the country. Drawing on decades of experience in the maritime industry, Captain Stossel said the country is experiencing the peak of the south-easterly monsoon season, which runs from May
item.content:encoded:
Papua New Guinea is now in the most dangerous period of the year for sea travel, and veteran Chief Marine Pilot Captain Max Stossel is urging people to avoid unnecessary journeys as rough weather continues across the country.

Drawing on decades of experience in the maritime industry, Captain Stossel said the country is experiencing the peak of the south-easterly monsoon season, which runs from May to October and brings strong trade winds, rough seas and large waves, particularly along the north and south coastlines.

He explained that Papua New Guinea experiences two monsoon seasons every year. The north-westerly monsoon, from December to March, brings heavy rain and thunderstorms, while the south-easterly monsoon creates stronger winds that make sea travel especially dangerous for small boats.

His warning comes after several recent maritime accidents, including the East New Britain incident involving 27 people, the rescue of eight people from a drifting dinghy off Madang by Pacific Towing's tug Koranga, and other incidents reported in Manus, Milne Bay and Western Province.

Captain Stossel said these incidents should serve as a reminder for people to pay close attention to weather forecasts before travelling.

"We are now in the peak of the south-easterly monsoon. These are strong seasonal winds, and if people do not need to travel, they should wait until the weather improves," he said.

Captain Stossel said many people continue to rely on small fibreglass dinghies, commonly known as banana boats, because they are often the only means of transport available to coastal and island communities.

He explained that these boats have a small draft, meaning only a small part of the hull sits below the water. While this makes them suitable for calm coastal waters and rivers, it also makes them light and less stable in rough seas.

According to Captain Stossel, when banana boats are overloaded with passengers and cargo, they are no match for strong winds and heavy waves.

"A banana boat is simply too light to compete with strong winds and big waves. Once it is overloaded, the risk of capsizing becomes much higher," he said.

Captain Stossel said many people are not travelling for leisure but because they need to reach hospitals, schools, banks, government offices and markets.

He said the lack of basic services in many remote communities forces people to travel even during dangerous weather conditions.

He believes the long-term solution is for the government to improve essential services in rural areas while investing in safer and more reliable passenger ferry services.

Captain Stossel said larger ferries are designed for open sea conditions, are more stable, carry trained crews and lifesaving equipment, and can safely transport more passengers than small dinghies.

"If we want to reduce the number of lives lost at sea, we must invest in proper ferry services and improve basic services in our rural communities. People should not have to risk their lives just to reach a hospital or buy food," he said.

"Airlines are becoming too expensive. Ferry service is the only solution. That's the only solution; there's no other solution. Banana boat is not the solution. Government should seriously look into this."

Captain Stossel also said stronger public awareness and responsible decision-making by boat operators and passengers are essential, especially during the current peak monsoon season.

He urged all coastal travelers to check weather forecasts, carry lifejackets for every passenger, and delay travel whenever sea conditions are unsafe. He said one careful decision before leaving the shore could save many lives.

item.title: 30-year wait ends for human rights
item.description: Papua New Guinea’s Department of Justice and Attorney-General [DJAG] has launched the long-awaited National Human Rights Policy in Port Moresby, ending a nearly 30-year wait for a national oversight framework. The human rights policy was launched in partnership with the European Union [EU] and the United Nations [UN].
item.content:encoded:
Papua New Guinea’s Department of Justice and Attorney-General [DJAG] has launched the long-awaited National Human Rights Policy in Port Moresby, ending a nearly 30-year wait for a national oversight framework.

The human rights policy was launched in partnership with the European Union [EU] and the United Nations [UN].

The policy aims to translate constitutional guarantees into practical protections for citizens across the country, with a focus on law and order, gender-based violence [GBV], land rights, and access to public services.

EU Ambassador to PNG, Erica Hasznos said the policy was the result of an inclusive consultative process involving civil society, churches, traditional leaders, and state agencies.

“This is a very important day in the sense that we have a human rights policy in place,” Hasznos said.

“It is good to have a policy, but it is even better to have action based on this policy. The EU will stand by Papua New Guinea as a committed partner to turn this policy into real action.”

Hasznos said the EU has committed K7 million in direct support for human rights projects.

This includes funding to draft constitutional amendments, set up the future National Human Rights Commission, and support the ongoing K50 million EU Spotlight Initiative targeting gender-based violence.

UN Resident Coordinator Shalini Bahuguna commended the Marape-Rosso government for taking a whole of government and society approach to address human rights issues.

“The Constitution of Papua New Guinea is amongst the world’s strongest in terms of human rights protection,” Bahuguna said.

“This policy translates those constitutional guarantees into real, practical results for people, whether children can attend school, women are protected from violence, or communities can access justice.”

Bahuguna said the real work now moves to implementation at the provincial, district, and ward levels.

DJAG Deputy Secretary for Legal Policy, E’ava Geita said the department accepts the responsibility of leading the national implementation.

Geita outlined DJAG's four strategic pillars under the plan:

Establishing the National Human Rights Commission; Building institutional capacity across state agencies; Fostering cross-sectoral partnerships; and, Enforcing strict monitoring through a National Mechanism for Implementation, Reporting, and Follow-up [NMIRF].

“This has been a long and arduous journey spanning over three decades,” Geita said. “With the formal launch of this policy, our focus shifts decisively from design to rigorous implementation.”

item.title: Appeal for greater maritime safety in Madang Province
item.description: A concerned senior citizen on Madang's Karkar Island is calling for greater maritime safety in the province. Tony Dibul, a former captain in the PNG Defence Force, made the call this week following the recent sea mishaps in the country's maritime provinces.
item.content:encoded:
A concerned senior citizen on Madang's Karkar Island is calling for greater maritime safety in the province.

Tony Dibul, a former captain in the PNG Defence Force, made the call this week following the recent sea mishaps in the country's maritime provinces.

"As an ordinary citizen who has travelled extensively by small craft throughout Madang Province over many years, I feel compelled to speak out on an issue that continues to put unnecessary lives at risk.

"Far too many boat operators continue to ignore maritime safety advisories, weather broadcasts, and the most basic safety requirements before putting to sea. This attitude is becoming increasingly dangerous and unacceptable," he said.

Just this past weekend, one dinghy carrying eight persons on board submerged and drifted from Saidor to Vidar before those on board were rescued. In another separate incident, another dinghy capsized outside Vidar.

Mr Dibul added, "Thankfully, no lives were lost in either incident, but that should not give us comfort. Instead, it should serve as a serious warning.

He said every one of these incidents trigger search and rescue operations involving volunteers, government agencies, and other boat operators who willingly risk their own lives to save others.

Mr Dibul further stated that these operations consume valuable time, fuel, equipment, and public resources. They expose rescuers to the very same dangerous sea conditions that caused the emergency in the first place.

The question we must ask ourselves is simple.

How many more warnings and near tragedies will it take before we change our attitude towards maritime safety?

"I commend the Madang Provincial Small Craft Registry Board for the progress it has made in registering small craft throughout the province. Registration is an important step towards improving maritime safety.

"However, registration alone is not enough.

"The Board, together with the responsible maritime authorities, must now place equal emphasis on enforcing the safety requirements that accompany registration.

"Compliance with maritime safety standards should not be treated as optional," he emphasised.

He said boat operators who continue to ignore weather and sea condition warnings, overload their vessels beyond safe carrying capacity, operate without sufficient life jackets for every passenger, fail to carry the required safety equipment, and operate vessels that do not comply with safety requirements should be prevented from departing.

"Where operators deliberately disregard these requirements and place lives at risk, the relevant authorities should not hesitate to prosecute offenders under the applicable maritime laws.

"Saving lives must take precedence over convenience or commercial gain," Dibul stated.

To passengers, Mr Dibul said that they also have a responsibility.

"Do not board a boat that is overloaded. Do not board a vessel that lacks life jackets or appears unsafe. If weather conditions are poor, postpone your journey. No appointment, cargo, or fare is worth a human life.

"For too long, we have accepted preventable maritime incidents as part of life along our coastline. They are not. Most of these incidents can be avoided if operators obey the law, respect the sea, and put safety first, he stressed.

Dibul clarified that he made this appeal not to criticise anyone but because he has witnessed too many unnecessary emergencies and too many rescue operations that could have been avoided.

"The sea will always command our respect. It does not forgive complacency, carelessness, or ignorance.

He appealed to everyone, including boat owners, operators, passengers, and authorities, to work together in order to ensure that every voyage begins safely and ends safely.

"One preventable death at sea is one too many," he said.

item.title: Tukana returns home as free community screenings tour Bougainville
item.description: One of Papua New Guinea's most celebrated films, Tukana – Husat I Asua, is returning to the big screen in Bougainville, with a series of free community screenings beginning on Wednesday, July 30. The tour will open in Tinputz, the home of the late Albert Toro, whose life inspired the iconic film. From there, screenings will travel to Hutjena in Buka on July 31, Arawa Independence Park on August 1,
item.content:encoded:
One of Papua New Guinea's most celebrated films, Tukana – Husat I Asua, is returning to the big screen in Bougainville, with a series of free community screenings beginning on Wednesday, July 30.

The tour will open in Tinputz, the home of the late Albert Toro, whose life inspired the iconic film. From there, screenings will travel to Hutjena in Buka on July 31, Arawa Independence Park on August 1, and conclude at the Mamaromino Women's Resource Centre in Buin on August 3.

Set in Bougainville, Tukana tells a compelling story of tradition, identity, leadership, and social change. Since its original release in the 1980s, the film has become a landmark in Papua New Guinea's cinematic history, resonating with audiences across generations.

The community screenings aim to bring people together to celebrate Bougainville's rich cultural heritage while introducing the restored classic to a new generation of viewers.

The film was recently digitally restored by the Papua New Guinea National Film Institute [NFI] in partnership with the Australian National Film and Sound Archive and Spectrum Films. The restoration was presented as a gift from the Australian Government to Papua New Guinea to commemorate the country's 50th Independence Anniversary.

The Bougainville screening tour is a joint initiative of the PNG National Film Institute and the Bougainville Arts, Culture and Tourism Authority. The program is supported by the Governments of Australia and New Zealand as part of their ongoing partnership with the Autonomous Bougainville Government to preserve and promote Bougainville's arts, culture and identity.

All screenings are free and open to the public.

item.title: Water provided for government institutions and communities in Tari
item.description: Two 10,000-litre water trucks are now operational in Tari, delivering emergency water to critical institutions and communities affected by the prolonged El Niño drought.
